title: Proposal for matter-wave interferometry with a rare-earth-doped microparticle
abstract: Matter-wave interferometers are sensitive probes of low energy physics and have been used for precise tests of gravity and quantum mechanics. These applications would benefit from interfering particles of higher mass, but observing the interference of a large particle is challenging due to the need to control its initial state and to avoid decoherence. Here we propose to demonstrate matter-wave interference of a microparticle with an embedded rare-earth ion. Optical transitions of the rare-earth ion will impart momentum to the microparticle's center of mass. The use of a time-symmetric interferometer geometry and a rare-earth ion state with angular momentum $J = 1/2$ will eliminate sensitivity to the initial conditions of the microparticle. We show that the rates of all relevant external decoherence mechanisms either decrease or remain constant as the microparticle mass is increased, allowing decoherence to be avoided by using sufficiently large particles. An apparatus at moderate vacuum levels will support microparticle interferometry with up to $10^3$ photons per beam splitter and millisecond coherence time. This demonstration will establish microparticle interferometry as a new platform for quantum sensing, improving searches for minimal modifications of quantum mechanics by up to four orders of magnitude in the near term and laying the foundation for future gravitational tests.
summary: This paper proposes a novel platform for matter-wave interferometry by embedding rare-earth ions within microparticles. It theoretically addresses the major hurdle of decoherence by showing that increasing the particle mass can suppress environmental decoherence rates. The result establishes a pathway for building quantum sensors capable of testing fundamental physics with unprecedented sensitivity.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing matter-wave interferometry using large, massive particles to enable precise tests of fundamental physics, which is severely limited by decoherence.
main_result: The proposal demonstrates that using rare-earth ions in microparticles, combined with specific interferometer geometries, allows decoherence rates to decrease or remain constant as particle mass increases, enabling high-precision sensing.
method: The work combines theoretical analysis of decoherence mechanisms (from background gas and blackbody radiation) with a proposed experimental setup utilizing optical Raman transitions on embedded rare-earth ions.
model_or_system: The system is a matter-wave interferometer using a microparticle doped with a rare-earth ion (e.g., Sm3+ in SrSe). The interference phase is read out via the quantum state of the ion, and decoherence is modeled by analyzing scattering interactions between the particle and the environment.
key_observables: Phase sensitivity ($\phi/g$), coherence time ($T$), decoherence rate ($\Gamma$), and the macroscopicity parameter ($\mu$).
important_parameters: Microparticle mass ($m$), vacuum level (moderate vacuum), photon count ($\sim 10^3$), and the rare-earth ion's angular momentum state ($J=1/2$).
main_assumptions: Decoherence due to blackbody radiation is assumed negligible, and the analysis relies on specific limits for the ratio between path separation ($\Delta x$) and momentum exchange wavelength ($\lambda$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Mach-Zehnder interferometer sequence using Raman transitions and show the calculated decoherence rate due to optical photon scattering as a function of microparticle mass.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for high-mass interferometry, then details the physical system using rare-earth ions and optical transitions. It proceeds to analyze decoherence from various sources (gas, BBR, optical), deriving theoretical models for the rate dependence on mass and path separation.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it merges quantum optics, solid-state physics, and quantum sensing. The detailed analysis of decoherence scaling with mass and the use of embedded quantum emitters (rare-earth ions) in solid-state hosts provide a concrete, advanced platform for studying open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental concept. Left: Mach-Zehnder interfer- ometry sequence of a microparticle with embedded rare-earth ion. The rare-earth ion interacts with three optical pulses. The interferometer phase, encoded in the state of the rare- earth ion after the interferometer, is sensitive to the acceler- ation of the microparticle. Right: diagram of Raman transi- tions used to implement the interferometer beam splitter and mirror pulses. The rare-earth ion remains in a state with total angular momentum J = 1/2 throughout the interferometer, which decouples the state of the rare-earth ion from the mi- croparticle’s orientation.

FIG. 2. Imaging scheme. The samarium ion is initially pumped to the 6P3/2 level, which decays non-radiatively to the 6P5/2 level. This level decays non-radiatively to the 4G5/2 level and radiatively to levels in the 6F and 6H manifolds. These levels can be repumped via 6P3/2 to enable optical cy- cling. Figure is not to scale.

Estimated decoherence rate of 2ℏk interferometer (light blue) and 1000ℏk interferometer (dark blue) due to background gas scattering as a function of microparticle mass, assuming 10−6 Torr pressure at 6 K. Dashed red line: deco- herence rate of 103 s−1, the maximum rate at which coherence can be observed after 1 ms.

Fig. 3 shows the estimated decoherence rate due to background gas scattering in an apparatus with buffer gas pressure 10−6 Torr as a function of particle mass for 2ℏk and 1000ℏk beam splitter momentum. The in- terferometer time is chosen to be T = 1 ms. The de- coherence rate of each interferometer has a local maxi- mum where ∆x ≈λHe. For sufficiently massive particles (m > 10−14 kg, corresponding to a microparticle of di- ameter 2 µm), this decoherence rate is slow enough to permit the observation of interference with 1000ℏk beam splitters.
